When something is abiding, it means it has lasted for a very long time — and continues to last — without weakening, fading, or disappearing. It describes something so deep and firmly rooted that it has essentially become a permanent part of someone's inner life or a situation's character.

Think of it this way: most things in life come and go. A mood passes. An enthusiasm fades. But an abiding feeling or quality stays. It survives the years. It survives change. It is still there, just as strong, long after many other things have come and gone.

The word carries two ideas at once, and both matter:

  1. Duration — it has lasted a long time, and is expected to keep lasting.
  2. Depth — it isn't shallow or surface-level. An abiding feeling is one that runs deep into a person's character or experience.

This combination is what gives "abiding" its weight. It doesn't just mean old or long-lasting in a neutral sense. It suggests something genuine, sincere, and deeply settled.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Abiding"?

"Abiding" almost always describes internal or abstract things — feelings, beliefs, interests, values, memories, and qualities — rather than physical objects.

You will most commonly see it paired with things like:

  • Love — an abiding love for her family
  • Interest or passion — an abiding interest in astronomy
  • Faith — an abiding faith in human goodness
  • Respect — an abiding respect for his mentor
  • Memory or impression — an abiding memory of that summer
  • Friendship — an abiding friendship built over decades
  • Principle or commitment — an abiding commitment to honesty
  • Hatred or resentment — an abiding hatred for injustice (it works for strong negative feelings too, though it's more commonly used for positive ones)

Notice a pattern: these are all things that live inside a person, or in the essence of a relationship or situation. They are not things you can touch or measure, but they are deeply real.

"She has an abiding love for classical music."
→ This love has been with her for most of her life. It hasn't dimmed. Even if she goes months without listening, the love is still there, deep inside her. It is part of who she is.

"He developed an abiding interest in the stars as a child, and it never left him."
→ This isn't a passing curiosity. He has been fascinated by the stars for decades, and that fascination is still alive and strong.

"The tragedy left an abiding sense of loss in the community."
→ Years later, the grief and the feeling of loss haven't gone away. They have settled into the community's memory permanently.

"They share an abiding friendship that has survived many hardships."
→ Their friendship has endured through difficult times and has only grown deeper. It is not going anywhere.

"She had an abiding belief that kindness matters more than anything else."
→ This belief has been at the core of how she lives her life, consistently, for as long as anyone can remember.

• It does not mean something that is merely old or ancient in a physical sense. You would not say "an abiding building" to mean a building that has stood for centuries. The word doesn't work well for physical objects.
  • It does not mean something that is just stubbornly continuing in an annoying way (that would be closer to persistent or chronic).
  • It does not describe something temporary, passing, fleeting, or fickle — those are the opposite of abiding.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words overlap with "abiding," but each has its own flavor:

  • Lasting is more neutral and general — it simply means something continues for a long time. A lasting impression. There is no sense of depth, and it can describe physical things just as easily.
  • Enduring is close, but it often implies surviving hardship or difficulty — things that have been tested and have held on. An enduring legacy. It also applies more comfortably to external things (a legacy, a structure, a work of art).
  • Deep-rooted emphasizes how firmly something is anchored, but doesn't necessarily say anything about how long it has lasted.
  • Persistent can have a slightly negative or neutral tone — a persistent problem, a persistent cough. It stresses continuation more than depth or sincerity.

Abiding is the most personal and emotionally resonant of this group. It quietly tells you that something has become woven into the fabric of who someone is, or what something stands for — not just that it has been around for a while.

"Abiding" has a somewhat formal and literary quality. You won't often hear it in very casual everyday conversation ("I have a real abiding love for pizza" would sound a bit odd and over-serious). It fits naturally in writing, in thoughtful speech, in literature, and when you want to express something with genuine weight and sincerity. When someone uses "abiding," it signals that they are being deliberate — that they mean this feeling or quality is not trivial or fleeting, but truly deep and lasting.

If you need to remember just one thing: abiding describes a feeling, belief, interest, or quality that has remained deeply and genuinely present in someone — or in a situation — over a long period of time, showing no sign of weakening or fading.
